title: How work runs: batches, dispatch, reviews, rulings

entries.summary: Ask the user when information is missing. Do not assume.
The backlog drives all work. Select backlog items before you start; every requirement traces to an item.
body: The backlog lives in `backlog/` (JSON). Read it with `houserules list --open`, `get <id>`, `batch <n>`; tick items with `set <id> status=done batch=<n>`.

entries.summary: A task brief carries every test, gate, and file its spec task names; an implementer who cannot satisfy one flags it instead of dropping it.
body: The controller writes briefs from the spec and plan; a silent omission surfaces only in review, one round late (batch 3, task 3).
When a brief and the spec disagree, the spec wins and the disagreement is a ruling to record.

source.ref: batch 3 branch review, uncovered_findings; task 3 review, finding 2

entries.summary: Start each batch with a brainstorming session or a written spec; get the user's approval before implementing.
body: Use the superpowers brainstorming and spec skills when the plugin is installed; otherwise write the spec by hand. Specs live in `docs/specs/`.
The order is strict: spec, then plan. A plan written before its approved spec is nil - deleted and the planning phase redone from the spec, never re-anchored (owner ruling, batch 18, 2026-09-05).

entries.summary: Commits use Conventional Commits (feat, fix, chore, test, ci, docs, refactor). Header at most 100 characters, body lines at most 100.
body: Start the subject in lowercase; a subject that starts with an uppercase token fails common commitlint configurations.

A commit whose author name ends in `[bot]` (Dependabot, any GitHub App) is exempt from the body-line limit alone: its body is generated and carries compare links no human wraps. Its subject and the trailer rules still apply.

entries.summary: Merge fast-forward only, from the CLI, after aggregating the branch into clean logical commits. No merge commits, no GitHub squash merges.
body: Aggregate with `git reset --soft $(git merge-base main HEAD)` and recommit in one to five Conventional Commits when interactive rebase is not available.
The project skill `finishing-a-feature` is the procedure.

entries.summary: Before you change a file, read its knowledge: the ids in your task and `houserules for <path>`. Cite the ids you relied on in your report.
Every ruling goes to its home file in the same turn — a deferral’s backlog item included. A ledger and the chat are not home files; neither survives compaction.
body: Home files: scope or product rulings go to a backlog entry; process rulings to a knowledge entry (`standing: true` when non-negotiable); design rulings to the batch spec.
A ledger note may accompany a ruling; it never substitutes for the tracked write.
A dispatch deviation from the spec's process line (model, order, gate) is a ruling: amend that spec line in the same turn. The batch report at the tick repeats it; it does not replace it.
An accepted implementer deviation is a ruling. Home it (a spec amendment or a backlog item) in the turn it is accepted, before the next dispatch.

A code comment is not a home file: a sanctioned deviation homes in the spec's deviations section or the design record the turn it is accepted; the comment may cite that home, never substitute for it (batch 16 task 4).

entries.summary: Run all agent work strictly sequentially. Never dispatch two implementers or two reviewers at the same time.
body: Parallel dispatches conflict in the working tree and hide which run produced a change.

entries.summary: Test-driven development for every executable change: the failing test first, or a disclosed-mutation proof for already-correct behavior; verbatim RED and GREEN.
body: Data-only and docs-only changes carry no RED/GREEN. The report's `tests` names the gates that ran instead (`kb check`, `backlog check`, `validate`, render drift, lint); the reviewer judges their sufficiency.
A data change with a testable consumer — a check pattern with a regression test, a rendered artifact a test pins — is a code change for this rule: the consumer test comes first.
A new test for behavior that is already correct proves it can fail through a deliberate, disclosed mutation, not a natural RED.
Never fabricate a cycle: an empty `tdd` with named gates is honest evidence; a manufactured RED is not.

A fix round that narrows or widens matching behavior carries its own RED or counter-example test. A cycle captured after the commit says so in the report's tdd entry and presents the runs in the order they really happened.
When no assertion can change (an output-noise or report-only fix), disclosed before/after captures of the observable difference are the honest evidence, presented in the order they ran.

The `mode` label follows when the shown run happened, not the failure's flavor: `natural` only when the shown RED ran pre-commit; a post-hoc recapture is `reconstructed` and the tdd entry says so; a disclosed-mutation proof is `mutation`.

Two label failures are ruled (batch 18): a mutation proof's RED shows the test FAILING under the mutation — a capture showing the tests passing proves nothing; and a post-commit recapture is `reconstructed` regardless of what also ran earlier — the label follows the shown run, and one report uses one label for one procedure.

entries.summary: Every review runs on a mightier model than the implementer it reviews. Implementers use the cheapest model that fits the task.
body: Model order: haiku < sonnet < opus < fable. Mightier is strict: an Opus implementer needs a Fable review, so choosing an Opus implementer is a deliberate, costed decision.
Scoped re-reviews follow the same bar as first reviews: the fix diff's size never lowers the reviewer's tier.
Name the model on every dispatch; an omitted model inherits the session's most expensive one.

entries.summary: Fix every review finding, Minor included. Defer a fix only for a stated reason, as a backlog item; never as a TODO in code.
body: Technical debt is a no-go. A finding a reviewer filed is fixed in the same fix round, whatever its severity.
The only way to defer: a backlog item that states the reason and the follow-up; the finding names the item. A ledger line or a chat note is not a deferral.
No `TODO`, `FIXME`, or `HACK` marker in source files; the deterministic check fails the audit on a new one. Todos live in `backlog/`.

entries.summary: Every plan carries a code-health scan of the files the batch touches: name the smells and antipatterns found, and fold targeted fixes into the tasks.
body: The goal is active maintenance. The Boy Scout Rule: leave the code cleaner than you found it. Visible neglect invites more neglect, so entropy is fought at every touch, not in rescue projects.

During brainstorming and plan writing, read the files the batch will change and list: code smells (duplication, long functions or files, divergent change, shotgun surgery, feature envy, primitive obsession, data clumps, speculative generality), antipatterns, and deviations from current best practice (verified against current docs, not memory).

Fold the fixes in as opportunistic refactoring: a step inside the task that touches the file, or a dedicated task when the cleanup is load-bearing. Where a cleanup makes the feature change easy, do it first.
Scope bound: only code the batch touches or directly depends on. An improvement outside that scope becomes a backlog item, never plan scope creep.
The scan's output is part of the plan: a Code health section naming the findings, what the plan fixes, and what goes to the backlog and why. A clean scan states what was checked.

This rule never justifies over-engineering: no abstraction for one caller, no configurability without a second use, no rewrite of working code the batch does not touch. Speculative generality is itself a smell.

entries.summary: Task reports, reviews, and branch reviews are JSON files that pass `houserules validate` against `.claude/schemas/deliverables.json`.
body: Every deliverable an agent writes is structured data in the batch workspace: `task-<N>-report.json`, `task-<N>-review.json`, `task-<N>-review-r<R>.json`, `branch-review.json`. The `kind` field names the definition.
Write the file, run `houserules validate <file>`, fix every error, then audit. A deliverable that does not validate is incomplete; the controller re-dispatches.

The implementer's `self_audit` starts as `null` and holds the audit's `summary` and deterministic rows after the audit; the check below fails until it does. `self_audit` always covers the whole task (`BASE..HEAD` at report time); a fix round's audit over the fix diff goes into that `fix_rounds` entry's `tests`.
`houserules stats` and the branch retrospective read these files; prose is invisible to them.

entries.summary: Re-run every `.claude/evals/` scenario when the implementer or task-reviewer template or a scenario changes; append the run to `.claude/evals/record.json`.
body: The scenarios are the regression suite for the agent templates. The check is a `co-change`: a change to `.claude/agents/implementer.md`, `.claude/agents/task-reviewer.md`, or `.claude/evals/*.json` without a change to `.claude/evals/record.json` fails the audit. The entry routes through the `docs` area (`.claude/**`), so every audit that touches the templates carries it without `--ids`; the `process` area has no paths.

Run every scenario in a detached scratch worktree at the branch head before the branch review; the orchestrating skill holds the procedure. Keep nothing from a worktree; workspace artifacts carry the `eval-` prefix.

A run set in the record names `date`, `templates` (the git blob id of each template under test from `git rev-parse HEAD:<path>`; blob ids survive commit aggregation, commit SHAs do not), and one row per scenario: `scenario`, `agent`, `model`, `pass`, `of`, `notes`. The branch reviewer compares the latest blob ids with `HEAD`.

No scenario covers `branch-reviewer` or the orchestrating skill; a change there needs no run. The `houserules render` command's own retrieval-protocol text shapes the generated skill the implementer loads; run the scenarios after a change there too — the check cannot see it.

A batch that edits templates in several tasks may pay with one end-of-batch run scheduled in the spec; each interim audit then carries the expected fail row, disclosed in the report's concerns; the branch does not merge before the record commit lands, and the branch-range audit is the row that must pass (batches 7-11, 14).

A template-touching batch may book ONE shared rerun at the final template state instead of a rerun per task (the ledgered economy); each interim task audit's deterministic fail is then recorded plan-mandated, citing the spec section that books the rerun, and the branch-range audit after the record commit is the row that must pass.

entries.summary: Verify a change live (run the app, service, or tool for real; capture evidence) before any PR, merge, or deploy spend.
body: CI and deploy runs cost money and time; a live run catches what unit tests cannot. Record the project's live-run recipe as a `procedure` entry.

entries.summary: Add knowledge future sessions need to `knowledge/`; session memory is not portable, repo files are.
body: Write the entry in the same turn you learn the fact. Then run `houserules render` and commit the generated files with it.

entries.summary: Create a project skill (`.claude/skills/`) for a repeatable procedure. Author it with the writing-skills skill when available.
A contract change migrates every earlier report in-batch: a report-only refresh round per task, a scoped re-review, and scripted checks for mechanical fixes.
body: Plan the sweep at pre-flight: refresh rounds run right after the contract task closes and before the next task dispatch, so every later review reads a valid workspace (batch 7 ran them after T4, before T5).

Semantic decisions in a refresh (which tdd mode, which narrative) belong to the task's reviewer, not the refresh dispatch: batch 7's controller over-steered one mode and the re-reviewer had to correct it.

Controller verification replaces a further review round only for reviewer-prescribed mechanical edits whose expected outcome the reviewer pre-verified; it is scripted (byte-equal audit rows, field presence), gated with && chains, and logged in the ledger. Judged findings always get a real review round.
The branch review reads the full workspace regardless, so the sweep is auditable end to end.

entries.summary: Seeded-violations fixtures follow fixed steps: seed violations in the eval worktree, doctor the report to hide only those fail rows, keep the true audit aside.
body: Seed at least two rule violations of different check types (batch 7: a range devDependency for exact-pins plus a null dependency_vetting) in one small commit inside the detached eval worktree.

Doctor the report minimally: remove only the seeded fail rows from self_audit, adjust the summary counts to match, and let the prose claim compliance — the reviewer must prove the edit by row arithmetic against a fresh run.
Keep the undoctored audit output outside the workspace the reviewer reads (batch 7: the session scratchpad), so the judge can score expected_behavior against ground truth.

The reviewer dispatch carries the identical Knowledge:/Backlog:/--ids block as a real task review; artifacts carry the eval- prefix in the batch workspace and the record append names both template blob ids.

entries.summary: Chain every evidence-producing shell sequence with && or explicit exit checks; an unchained tail after a heredoc reports success for a command that never ran.
body: Batch 7 hit the class twice: a heredoc-tail slip forced an amend, and a follow-up verification printed a success message while the evidence append was silently skipped; both were caught only because the output was re-read.
Write verification scripts so the success message is unreachable when any prior command fails: && chains, or a trailing explicit exit-code check per command. set -e does not protect tool-run shells.
Re-run, do not hand-repair, any evidence produced by a sequence that later proves unchained.
Output redirection placed after an && chain binds only the last command; wrap the chain in a subshell, or redirect per command, when the whole sequence is the evidence (batch 9).
A zero-count probe (grep -c) exits nonzero on zero matches and breaks the chain even when zero is the expected answer; gate count probes on their output, not their exit (batch 9).

A before/after evidence bracket (snapshot, action, snapshot, diff) is one && chain in one call; snapshots captured across separate calls prove nothing about order. Re-run the whole bracket, never splice it, and check the artifact mtimes increase in chain order (batch 10).

entries.summary: On a backlog collision with main, main wins: rebuild the branch on it by cherry-pick, drop the never-merged branch filings, and park superseded analysis.
body: Batch 13: an owner-side agent merged HR-047/048 to main while the branch carried candidate filings under the same ids. Never-merged branch-local filings can be dropped without breaching knowledge-base.ids-are-permanent.
Verify overlap yourself with git diff --name-only on both sides; another agent's no-overlap claim is a claim, not evidence.
Record the old-to-new sha map in a workspace file and the batch report: closed tasks' deliverables keep pre-rebuild shas, and gc can prune those objects.

source.ref: batch 13 branch review; the HR-047/048 collision

entries.summary: Owner content found uncommitted on the shared tree mid-batch: commit it verbatim as its own commit, surface concerns instead of editing, record its position.
body: Batch 14: the README convergence paragraphs surfaced while T1 ran; secured as their own docs(readme) commit, two notes surfaced to the owner (a dropped link, lowercase product names), nothing silently changed.

Verify the interleave position with git log before writing the ledger line: state which task commits sit below and above it. A wrong containment claim forces a ledger correction and changes which range the task review must read (batch 14 T1).
At aggregation the commit stays its own commit; no task diff absorbs it, and the task-review dispatch names it as owner content to be judged as such.

entries.summary: Cite evidence only at paths that outlive the session: the batch workspace or the tracked tree, never a session scratchpad.
body: A report or workspace doc that cites a capture must name a file under the batch workspace (or the repository) that a later reader can open. A session scratchpad path is dead the moment the session ends; a citation into it is a claim nobody can collect on.

Copy small captures into the workspace beside the doc that cites them (batch 16 task 5: 59 files under t5-evidence/). An artifact too large to retain is disclosed as not retained, with its decisive excerpt quoted inline - never cited at a path that no longer exists.
Truncation markers count as citations: a marker naming a full log must point at a durable file whose content is a byte-prefix match of the retained excerpt.

A long-lived SOURCE comment states the rerunnable command and its measured counts inline, self-contained; a batch-workspace path may ride along as provenance but never as the only evidence, because a clone carries no workspace (ruled at the batch 20 report, docs/design.md 5.52).

source.ref: batch 16 task 5 review finding 5; owner ruling at the batch 16 report

entries.summary: Before submitting a report, re-open every artifact a claim cites and confirm the artifact shows what the sentence says.
body: The recurring failure is not fabrication but drift: the work is right while the sentence describing it cites a capture that is not there, quotes a line the capture lost, or keeps a rationale a later verification overturned (batch 16 tasks 2 and 5).

The check is mechanical: for each named file, open it; for each quoted line, grep it; for each number, recompute it from the artifact. A reviewer does exactly this, so a report that skips it converts Minor findings into review rounds.
A reversed trend is worth recording too: name the pattern in the review when it appears, and name its reversal when a later round demonstrates it (batch 16 task 2 round 2).

A SHIPPED doc or comment sentence stating a measurement is a claim like a report sentence (ruled batch 18): it cites a retained capture at a durable path, and a fix round's sweep re-opens every doc sentence the round touched. The report-claims checker cannot see shipped files — the manual sweep is the only net there.

A command field is the literal command copied from the terminal — never retyped, never annotated inline; labels and notes go beside the field (ruled batch 19: the class failed four review rounds). A reviewer paste-runs command fields; a field that cannot paste-run is a finding by itself.

Close every report by running the report-claims checker (`houserules check-report-claims <REPORT_FILE>`) over the report file after the last edit, and paste its clean run as the final tests entry. The checker is a floor, not a substitute for the manual sweep: its Limits section (crates/houserules/src/report_claims.rs, reachable only where this kit's own source lives) names what only the sweep catches; an adopter repo carries no such source, so there a false positive is disclosed per report and reported upstream instead. It ships as a `houserules` subcommand (HR-066, batch 20 T2), so the closing act runs in every adopter repo, not only the one that built it. The checker gates gitignored workspace reports, never a tracked artifact a CI job could see, so it carries no CI job of its own -- the implementer template's closing-act mandate (HR-060) is the whole mechanism.

A commit message body is a claim like a report sentence: recompute its counts from the artifact before committing; a wrong count found post-commit is recorded in the report for aggregation to carry, never amended and never left silent (batch 20 carried five such corrections; commit prose was the largest surviving drift surface once the checker gated reports).

After any world-changing event - a fix round, an interruption, a rebase - re-derive every count and summary-scope field (implemented, self_review, doc comments citing measurements) from the tree at HEAD before re-submitting; a carried-forward sentence is a new claim, never trusted (batch 21: all four tasks failed this at least once; the interruption seam cost a full review round).

A claim about a failure names whether it was OBSERVED or INFERRED - a commit body keeps the same observed-vs-reconstructed split its report keeps (batch 21 branch-fix 2: the report drew the split correctly while a local-history commit body collapsed it into one 'panicked').

Five drift classes, each caught only by re-derivation across batch 22's five tasks: a rewritten command string that was never run as written; a count not re-measured after the change; a citation carrying a stream index where a file line belongs; a false universal ('every', 'all') no enumeration was run for; and a transcription of another agent's wording whose particulars were never checked against the tree.
Re-derive every sentence from the tree at the final HEAD immediately before the report ships; a sentence carried from a draft, a review, or a dispatch is re-derived before it lands.

source.ref: batch 16 task 2 re-review r1 trend note; owner ruling at the batch 16 report

entries.summary: A claim that a set is closed ('every', 'all', 'no remaining') names the bounded, rerunnable enumeration that produced it; without the artifact, no claim.
body: Born from the batch 17 argv-closure arc: every unenumerated closure sentence was false in at least one direction, and each fix was a script whose output the sentence could then cite.
The enumeration lives at a path that outlives the session and reruns cleanly; its own summary line states the counts the claim cites, so a reader checks the artifact, not the prose.

A migration or flip closure names its zero-hit sweep of the RETIRED form (the grep pattern and its variants), rerunnable at HEAD; the enumeration is of the old form's residue, not the new form's presence (ruled batch 19: presence enumerations confirm known work, only residue sweeps falsify closure — batch 18 T6 and batch 19 T2 both failed this way).

The enumeration artifact is executable: a script whose own run prints the counts the claim cites, not a static dump or a hand-asserted mapping (batch 20: an asserted mapping hid a live coverage drop; grep dumps matched no command at HEAD until an executable sweep replaced them; a /tmp list failed durability until the comparison reran from git history).

The enumeration's pattern derives from the claim's SUBJECT, widened to every spelling the corpus itself uses - run a spelling-discovery probe first and retain it - never from one artifact's name (batch 21: a name-keyed sweep missed six subject-spelling lines; a /tmp-only regex missed six scratchpad citations; a hand-asserted home list omitted a live home).

The enumeration names its corpus AND its pattern classes, and the pattern set derives from the corpus's own spellings: run a spelling-discovery probe first and retain it beside the verification script. Batch 22 hit all three failure sub-shapes - a spelling the pattern never tested for, an assigned file absent from the file list, and a marker class the script's own header claimed but did not encode.

source.ref: batch 17 report ruling; branch review retrospective

entries.summary: A review finding stating a measurement, a reproduction, or a proposed fix's behavior is verified by running it before filing; restated claims are re-derived.
body: Batch 17 caught the reviewer wrong twice (a prescribed device that provably did not work; a divergence tally measured with the wrong command names) and the controller's dispatch premises wrong twice - each caught only because someone re-ran the thing. The discipline that binds the implementer's report binds the review's findings and the dispatch's diagnosis alike.
The paired task-reviewer template clause lands with HR-060.

source.ref: batch 17 report ruling; branch review retrospective

entries.summary: Verify behavior against the persisted state the code reads in production; a one-off override is a different state and can falsify the measurement.
body: Batch 18 T2: `git -c core.commentChar=X commitlint --edit` measured 'both tools share the blind spot' because -c never persists and commitlint's `git config` lookup found nothing; with the value persisted in the repository's config, commitlint adapted and check-commit did not - the reversed measurement was the real finding and produced the fix.

Before citing a tool's behavior under configuration, persist the configuration the way a user would (config file, not a process-scoped flag or env var), then run both sides from that state. State the persistence mechanism in the capture.

source.ref: batch 18 T2 fix round 2 correction; task-2-review-r3.json re-derivation

entries.summary: A trigger, pin, or wiring check runs the resolution end to end - feed the produced value to its consumer; a string, glob, or schema match proves nothing.
body: The batch-19 shape: release.yml's tag glob matched v0.2.0-alpha, and dist plan --tag=v0.2.0-alpha still exited 255 because CARGO_PKG_VERSION could not resolve the tag - the pattern check passed while the pipeline was broken on every tag the flow would produce (batch 19 task-1-review.json issue 2).

The proof is the consumer's own run, captured: dist plan for a tag wiring, the updater's replacement count for a pin wiring, the as-CI shell for a workflow step. The match check stays as the cheap first gate, never the verdict.

A third-party breakage claim states WHEN it fires, derived from the pinned source's call path - never hedged as 'may fail' - because the hedge is what mis-schedules the fix (batch 20: HR-073's original wording queued a push-time failure behind a release-time track until the source derivation re-scoped it pre-merge).

entries.summary: No commit that lands on main may fail the ci.yml checked in beside it; sequence a migration's deletions or collapse the red range at aggregation.
body: A fast-forward merge lands every aggregated commit on main; a bisect, a revert target, or a checkout of any of them must build and pass the CI definition at that same commit.

Batch 20 T3: the corpus deletion commits satisfied the cargo-side flip-with-deletion rule at every commit, but the still-present JS gate (corpus.test.mjs) was red from the first deletion commit until the vitest layer itself retired - caught only by the reviewer's per-commit reproduction, and repaired at aggregation by collapsing the range into the deletion commit.

The check at aggregation time: for each collapsed commit, the gates its own ci.yml names run green; a migration that cannot keep an interim gate green retires that gate's subject in the same collapsed commit.

source.ref: batch 20 branch review; task-3-review.json important finding 1; T3 report concerns[10]

entries.summary: Another agent's suggested wording, pin, or count is a draft, not evidence: re-derive every number, quote, and reference from the tree before transcribing it.
body: A reviewer's finding text and a controller's course correction are claims by their authors; the agent who lands them owns their truth at the landing revision.

Origin: batch 22 T3a round 3 - a review's suggested wording carried line pins wrong in the suggestion itself, and the fix transcribed them unchecked; the repair dropped pins for stable function names.
This is the transcriber's half of process.review-findings-are-claims-too, which binds only the finding's author.

entries.summary: A fix round closes only with a written verification record: a re-review deliverable, or a controller note naming each finding and the artifact proving its fix.
body: A re-review deliverable in the workspace is the default for rounds with executable changes or any critical finding. A controller verification note suffices for report-only or prose rounds when it names finding-by-finding evidence.
Origin: batch 23 T2's fix round closed on a ledger note alone; the verifications were real and reproducible, but nothing pinned where such a record must live or what it must name.
